extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ (Boolean Questions) is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each question is paired with a paragraph from Wikipedia that contains the answer. The questions are generated in unprompted and unconstrained settings, meaning they were authored by people who were not prompted to write particular kinds of questions and who did not know the answer to the question they were asking. The dataset is designed to test models' ability to make complex, non-factoid inferences.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.publisher: Google AI Language and Paul G. Allen School of CSE, University of Washington
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1 [cs.CL] 24 May 2019
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results, in which case the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator for further processing.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia articles
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are heuristically filtered to identify yes/no questions by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words (did, do, does, is, are, was, were, have, has, can, could, will, would) and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The dataset combines 13k questions gathered from the pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set to reach a total of 16k questions. These are split into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good, meaning it is comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information. This judgment is made before the annotator sees the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question. Annotators can mark questions as not answerable if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is yes or no.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). There is a correlation between the nature of the question and the likelihood of a yes answer, though this correlation is too weak to help outperform the majority baseline. Question-only models perform very poorly on this task, which helps confirm that the questions do not contain sufficient information to predict the answer on their own.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to yes/no questions paired with single paragraphs from Wikipedia rather than entire documents, which helps reduce ambiguity but may not fully represent document-level understanding tasks. The questions are primarily about Wikipedia content, which may limit generalization to other domains. Human annotators achieved 90% accuracy, leaving a 10% margin that may represent inherently ambiguous or difficult cases.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating reading comprehension models on their ability to answer naturally occurring yes/no questions. It can be used to test models' inferential abilities, including complex, non-factoid reasoning and entailment-like inference. The dataset is split into training (9.4k examples), development (3.2k examples), and test (3.2k examples) sets.
